introduction-authority-vs-influence.core: Platform and staff engineers often need hundreds of people to change how they work without being able to order them to. Influence (earned trust, understanding people's interests, compelling problems) is the main lever.

first_principles.problem: A platform team mandates a new deploy tool, teams ignore or resist it, and adoption stalls.
truths: People adopt what solves their problems.

analogy.title: A gardener vs. a sculptor
analogy.story: You can't carve people into shape; you create the conditions in which the change grows.
analogy.breaks: Some changes (security, compliance) do need mandates, so influence and authority work together.

example.title: Two platform launches
flow: Influence: co-designed with 3 pilot teams, champions → 80%

check.q: Why do mandates often fail for platform adoption?
check.a: They produce reluctant compliance or resistance rather than genuine commitment.

the-foundation-social-capital.core: Influence is a by-product of trust built over time: delivering on promises, helping others without immediate return, sharing credit, listening and being consistently competent. It's social capital you draw on when you need people to follow.

first_principles.problem: An engineer new to the org proposes a big change, and nobody trusts them enough to try it.
truths: Trust grows through repeated positive interactions.
Reciprocity is a strong social norm.
derivation: **Listen** and build relationships before you need them.

analogy.title: A bank account of trust
analogy.story: Small deposits over time let you make a large withdrawal when you need support for a big change.
analogy.breaks: Social capital can be spent quickly through broken promises, so protect it.

example.title: Building capital before a big proposal

check.q: What is 'social capital' in the context of influence?
check.a: Accumulated trust and goodwill from past reliable, helpful behaviour that makes people willing to follow your proposals.

stakeholder-management-knowing-your-audi.core: Different stakeholders care about different things: developers want an easier workflow, managers want delivery speed, executives want cost and risk, security wants compliance. Map them by influence and interest, and tailor the message to each.

first_principles.problem: One generic pitch about 'our new platform' bores executives and doesn't convince developers.
truths: People evaluate change through their own goals.
Influence and interest vary by stakeholder.
derivation: **Tailor**: dev experience, delivery metrics, cost and risk.
**Engage** early: manage the high-power ones closely, keep others informed.

analogy.title: Pitching a house renovation to a family
analogy.story: Kids care about bedrooms, parents about the budget, grandparents about accessibility. One pitch doesn't fit all.
analogy.breaks: Tailoring must stay honest. Don't tell different groups contradictory stories.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each group sees its own win.

check.q: What does a power/interest grid help you decide?
check.a: How closely to engage each stakeholder, from managing closely to just keeping informed.

driving-change-selling-the-problem-not-t.core: Lead with the problem people already feel (with data), build shared agreement that it matters, and only then co-create the solution. People resist solutions to problems they don't believe they have.

first_principles.problem: 'We built an amazing service mesh, please adopt it' meets indifference, because nobody agreed there was a problem.
truths: People commit to solving problems they recognise.
Ownership of a solution grows from involvement.
derivation: **Quantify** the pain (incidents, lead time, toil hours).
**Socialise** the problem and get agreement it matters.

analogy.title: A doctor explaining a diagnosis before prescribing
analogy.story: Patients take medicine they understand they need; they ignore prescriptions for conditions they don't believe they have.
analogy.breaks: Some problems are invisible to those affected (security risk), so data and storytelling matter even more.

example.title: Problem-first pitch
flow: Data: average deploy takes 3h of engineer time, 12 incidents/qtr from manual steps

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Teams adopt because the solution is theirs.

example.outcome: change that's pulled by its users, not pushed onto them.

check.q: Why lead with the problem rather than the solution?
check.a: People commit to solutions for problems they recognise and helped define, rather than ones imposed on them.

navigating-resistance-and-conflict.core: Resistance usually has reasons: loss of control, extra work, fear of failure, past bad experiences or a genuinely better idea. Listen to understand it, address the concrete concerns, find shared goals and escalate constructively when needed.

first_principles.problem: Pushback is treated as obstruction, so conflict escalates and adoption stalls.
truths: People fear losing autonomy and competence.
derivation: **Listen** and ask 'what would make this work for you?'.
**Address** them: migration help, opt-outs, phased timelines.
**Disagree and commit**, or escalate with shared data when you're stuck.

analogy.title: A river meeting rocks
analogy.story: Water doesn't smash the rocks; it finds the path around, and sometimes the rock shows the better route.
analogy.breaks: Some resistance is pure politics, which may need leadership alignment.

example.title: A resistant team
flow: Concern: their custom GPU tests unsupported

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: A blocker turns into an ally.

check.q: Why treat resistance as information rather than obstruction?
check.a: It often reveals real concerns or better ideas that, once addressed, improve the change and its adoption.
